html:
Sir Syed Ahmad Khan was the leading Muslim reformer of 19th-century India. He founded the college at Aligarh and argued that Indian Muslims must take up modern education or be left behind.

He was born in Delhi in 1817 into a family close to the Mughal court and became a judge in the Company's service. In the Rebellion of 1857 he saved the British residents of Bijnor. Afterwards the British blamed Muslims most, and the old Muslim upper class of north India was ruined. He wrote a bold pamphlet, The Causes of the Indian Revolt, which put the blame on British policy.

His answer was to learn from the West. He started a society to translate science books into Urdu, spent seventeen months in England, and wrote that Islam, rightly understood, cannot conflict with science. Orthodox scholars, including those of Deoband, condemned him.

In 1875 he opened the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College at Aligarh on the model of Cambridge (see Aligarh college). It became a university in 1920.

He told Muslims to keep out of the Indian National Congress. In an elected system, he said, the Hindu majority would always win, and he spoke of Hindus and Muslims as two nations. The founders of the Muslim League came from Aligarh.
sum: Sir Syed Ahmad Khan was the leading Muslim reformer of 19th-century India. He founded the college at Aligarh and argued that Indian Muslims must take up modern education or be left behind.
